Decision lab

Compare the options.

Give each candidate a score from 0 to 3. 0 = not a match, 1 = maybe, 2 = good, and 3 = excellent. The totals update automatically.

01 / Habitat match

Does your yard have the kind of home this bird needs? Think about trees, shrubs, open sky, and nearby food.

  • Chickadee or nuthatch: trees and wooded areas help, especially evergreens.
  • Violet-green swallow: open flying space and insect-rich air are important.
  • House wren: shrubs, brushy edges, and shelter can help.
  • Northern flicker: mature trees and places to search for ants.
0 no suitable habitat · 1 a little · 2 quite a bit · 3 a strong match
Try thisLook at your yard sketch on chapter 3. Which bird has the most of what it needs?
02 / Bird sightings

Is the bird already visiting your yard or neighborhood? A bird seen nearby may be more likely to discover your box, but sightings are clues—not guarantees.

  • Watch quietly for 10 minutes in the morning or late afternoon.
  • Look and listen. Nuthatches climb trunks; flickers often feed on lawns; swallows fly above open areas.
  • Ask an adult to use Merlin Bird ID, or keep notes in your observation journal.
  • Swallows are seasonal: not seeing one in November does not mean it is absent in spring.
0 not seen or heard · 1 unsure or possible · 2 noticed nearby · 3 regularly observed
Try thisWrite down the date and location of each sighting. If the bird is migratory, ask about spring and summer sightings, too.
03 / Build difficulty

How realistic is this build for you and your adult helper? Here, a higher score means easier, not harder.

  • Small chickadee, nuthatch, and wren boxes: often simpler starter projects.
  • Swallow under-eave box: the box may be manageable, but mounting it safely under a roof needs planning.
  • Flicker box: larger pieces and a heavier installation can make it a harder first build.
0 too hard right now · 1 challenging · 2 manageable with help · 3 a good beginner build
Try thisOpen the Audubon plan together. Count the pieces, check the tools, and decide who will drill, cut, and mount it. Adults handle power tools and ladders.
04 / Space available

Is there a safe, suitable spot to put the finished box? This is about the actual mounting location, not the total size of your yard.

  • Can an adult reach a suitable pole, tree, or eave to mount and clean the box?
  • Is the entrance away from busy paths and easy access by cats or other predators?
  • Is there enough clear flight room for a swallow, or nearby tree cover for a forest bird?
  • Can you give the box suitable height and spacing, following the chosen plan?
0 no safe spot · 1 uncertain spot · 2 likely good spot · 3 clear, safe, plan-compatible spot
Try thisMark the possible location on the yard sketch. Ask your adult helper to confirm safe mounting and predator protection before giving it a 3.

08
Citizen science

Install & observe.

Install with an adult in a suitable location and watch from a distance. Never disturb an active nest.

Our birdhouse report
Our finished project
Try a photo of the birdhouse after installation. Do not open a box when eggs or nestlings are present.
Installation field notes — read before mounting
  • Height depends on the bird: chestnut-backed chickadees and red-breasted nuthatches usually 5–15 ft; house wrens 5–10 ft; violet-green swallows 9–15 ft; northern flickers 6–12 ft. Follow your exact plan.
  • Choose habitat, not just height: wooded shelter for chickadees and nuthatches, brushy edges for wrens, open flight space for swallows, and mature trees or forest edges for flickers.
  • Face the entrance away from prevailing winds where appropriate. Avoid intense afternoon sun and place the box away from busy doors, pets, and easy predator access.
  • Twigs or starter nests? Usually leave a nest box empty—the birds build their own nests. For chickadees or red-breasted nuthatches, about 1 inch of untreated wood shavings may be used. A flicker box is different: it should be filled with clean wood chips or shavings. Never pack in twigs or commercial nesting fluff.
  • Mount securely: an adult chooses suitable hardware, checks stability and predator protection, and performs all ladder work. A sturdy pole and predator guard may be safer than attaching directly to a living tree.
  • After installation: keep the box dry, ventilated and accessible for seasonal cleaning. Do not disturb active nests; observe from a distance.

Species placement reference: Cornell NestWatch — Nest Box Placement ↗. Mounting instructions in your chosen Audubon plan take priority.

09
Bonus / cold weather

A winter roost box.

Nesting boxes help birds raise chicks. Roost boxes are different: they can offer a sheltered place to rest during cold weather.

Illustrated idea

Conceptual illustration only. The downloadable Audubon design has the actual cut sizes and assembly requirements.

What makes it different?
  • It is for resting and staying sheltered, not raising babies.
  • A typical roost box puts the entrance lower than many nest boxes to help retain warmer air.
  • The box needs a clean-out method and a safe mount.
  • Use the published plan instead of copying this illustration's proportions.
Download the winter roost-box building plans (PDF) ↗ Visit the Audubon birdhouse plans page ↗
Winter shelter / Not a nesting house

Our bonus project follows its own design. Unlike a spring nest box, a winter roost box is made to shelter birds from the cold. Use the linked plan for exact dimensions and assembly.

Seasonal question

What do the birds need when it gets cold?

Food, water, protective cover, and safe places to rest are valuable habitat features—whether or not birds use a roost box.
